claims.text: Changing constituent percentages in HfNbTaTiZr while retaining the same alloy system will systematically change hardness and tensile strength.
The baseline HfNbTaTiZr alloy is uniform or equiatomic.
A controlled design-of-experiments approach can isolate the mechanical-property effects of changing selected constituent percentages.
Changing composition alters the local atomic configuration and elemental distribution in the microstructure.
Composition changes can alter phase stability.
Composition changes can alter defect structures.
Changing elemental proportions alters local bonding environments.
Changing elemental proportions alters atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion.
Changes in lattice distortion modify solid-solution strengthening.
The resulting strengthening changes influence dislocation mobility under mechanical stress.
Specific changes in constituent percentages will produce measurable and predictable increases or decreases in hardness and tensile strength.
Increasing the fraction of a larger-radius element that promotes lattice distortion may enhance strengthening up to a limiting point.
Simple compositional trends are expected only over a limited composition range before precipitation, phase separation, or new-phase formation intervenes.
The magnitude and direction of property changes depend on inter-element interactions and processing conditions.
Elemental-percentage effects may be nonlinear or exhibit thresholds.

contradictions.description: The intervention recognizes that increasing one elemental percentage requires decreasing another, whereas the experiment says one element will be varied independently while the total composition remains constant. Under the compositional sum constraint, an elemental fraction cannot literally vary independently unless the balancing adjustment is specified.
